name: Connecticut Mirror
title: CT Senate pulls all-nighter, rearranging budget and passing gun bill
description: The Senate stayed overnight to pass a gun control bill and legislation that revises the state’s already-adopted state budget
text:
The Senate stayed overnight at the state Capitol to pass a gun control bill and legislation that would make millions of dollars in revisions to the state’s recently adopted state budget and — among other things — delay Hartford’s revaluation by one year and help struggling Ansonia revive a failed and ruinously expensive fuel-cell project.
The budget revisions and unrelated changes to other bills and laws arrived Tuesday  afternoon in an 111-page amendment Democrats intended to tack onto an unrelated measure, Senate Bill 477. It ignited a Republican slowdown that pushed action on other bills well past midnight and into Wednesday morning, the final day of the legislature’s annual session.
“The Republicans dared us to go all night because they didn’t like a bill,” said Senate Majority Leader Bob Duff, D-Norwalk. “They thought we’d blink, and we didn’t.”
With 105 sections, the budget measure would increase judicial salaries by 4.5%, adjust film tax credits, increase Medicaid rates for optometrists, enable municipalities to abate certain delinquent taxes, increase funding for Shore Line East railroad service by at least $3 million and specify how $100 million in municipal grants would be shared by the state’s 169 cities and towns.
It also would place Sue Bird, the former University of Connecticut and WNBA basketball star, alongside the American robin as the state bird of Connecticut.
The Senate met until nearly 8 a.m., not leaving until passing House Bill 5043, controversial legislation banning the manufacture and sale of Glock handguns and other “convertible” firearms that can readily be made to function as an illegal machine gun.
Debate on the gun bill, a measure proposed by Gov. Ned Lamont, opened at 3:15 a.m. with no one in the public galleries. By 4:30 a.m., Sen. Rob Sampson, R-Wolcott, was debating Sen. Gary Winfield, D-New Haven, in a nearly empty chamber, and the Senate’s clerk seemed to briefly doze. Passage came at 7:22 a.m. on a 22-11 vote, with three senators missing.
Senate Majority Leader Bob Duff, left, and Senate President Pro Tem Martin Looney going to vote at 7:15 a.m. on May 6, 2026. Credit: mark pazniokas
The House had quit for the night at 10 p.m. Tuesday, scheduled to return at 10 a.m. Wednesday for the final 14 hours of the 2026 session. Among the bills awaiting them was the budget revision, S.B. 477, which passed the Senate on 25-11 party-line vote.
The bill was packed with new funding to nonprofits, their legislative benefactors unclear. Its breadth outraged Republicans on a day when the legislature’s tradition of unlimited debate allows the GOP minority to control the flow of business simply by talking.
Senate Minority Leader Stephen Harding, R-Brookfield, said the amendment to S.B. 477 essentially was a second budget implementation bill drafted just three days after the budget was adopted by the both the Senate and House.
The amendment was signed by the top Democratic leaders of the House and Senate, as well as the co-chairs of the Finance, Revenue and Bonding Committee.
Some of the provisions initially were hard to decipher, especially sections that seemed to neutralize jurisdiction by the Public Utilities Regulatory Authority and the Connecticut Siting Council over a $63.6 million fuel-cell project in Ansonia. 
“This is not how our state government should operate. It not an open, transparent and reasonable process,” said Sen. Ryan Fazio, R-Greenwich.
Under the administration of former Republican Mayor David Casetti, the financially strapped Ansonia sold its water and sewer system to Aquarion Water Co. for $41 million and got into the business of generating electricity with a fuel-cell project with a partner, Johnson Controls, located at 345 N. Main Street.
But there was a problem. As the Valley Independent Sentinel reported in March, the Connecticut Siting Council had already approved an application for a fuel cell at the same location from another company, HyAxiom out of South Windsor. But Cassetti never signed a final agreement with HyAxiom, questioning the financing.
He then made an agreement with Johnson Controls, agreeing to pay $37 million to the company to install the fuel cells. An obstacle to going forward is that the Siting Council’s approval rests with HyAxiom, not Johnson. A provision of S.B. 477 would negate the council’s approval.
Cassetti lost his reelection bid last year and was succeeded by a Democrat,  Frank Tyszka, who took office on Dec. 1 to find a surprise bill for nearly $700,000.  It was a payment due on the fuel cell, which was supposed to be up and running in 2025.
Harding said many of the provisions in the sweeping budget revisions violated arrangements made to keep business flowing.
“There were earmarks and absentee ballot changes never agreed to,” Harding said. “So, we’re fighting for our members to be able to have an opportunity to actually read bills before we vote on them. And part of that is talking on bills.”
And talk, they did.
Before S.B. 477 was called, Republicans spent six hours on Tuesday quizzing Sen. Christine Cohen, D-Guilford, co-chair of the Transportation Committee, about the contents of an omnibus transportation measure, House Bill 5464. It was theater, not real opposition. It passed easily, 32-4. Cohen posed for a photo by the tally board.
They turned to S.B. 477, which passed at 1:58 p.m., and then the gun bill. They passed a few other bills after the gun measure.
Senate President Pro Tem Martin M. Looney, D-New Haven, who is not seeking reelection after 46 years in the General Assembly, said, “We passed all the bills we planned to pass. It just took a little longer.”
Duff told the senators to return by 1:45 p.m. Wednesday for a group portrait, then more business.
“Dress sharp,” he said.

name: Nevada Current
title: Progressive incumbent challenged by urban planner in Assembly district that has the Strip
description: In Nevada State Assembly District 15, Democratic voters will decide whether to give their progressive incumbent a fifth term, despite his strained ties with some key labor groups. Incumbent Assemblymember Howard Watts is being challenged in the Democratic primary by Miguel Dávila, a political staffer turned urban planner. No Republican, third-party or indepe[...]
text:
Assemblymember Howard Watts (left) is being challenged in the Assembly District 15 Democratic primary by urban planner Miguel Dávila (right).In Nevada State Assembly District 15, Democratic voters will decide whether to give their progressive incumbent a fifth term, despite his strained ties with some key labor groups.
Incumbent Assemblymember Howard Watts is being challenged in the Democratic primary by Miguel Dávila, a political staffer turned urban planner. No Republican, third-party or independent candidates filed to represent the central Las Vegas Valley district, meaning whoever wins the Democratic primary will automatically win the November general election.
Watts has a significant fundraising advantage, according to campaign contribution and expense reports filed with the state. But Dávila’s run has been emboldened by endorsements from unions like AFL-CIO, LiUNA Laborers Local 872, and Teamsters Nevada, which have criticized Watts over legislative votes related to automation and tax subsidies for corporations. Dávila is also backed by SEIU, which he is a member of.
Watts told the Nevada Current he was “not going to speculate” on whether the support for Dávila is retaliation for any of his prior votes.
“If you look at my record on labor issues and issues related to workers, I have supported and done a lot,” said Watts. “I’ve worked hand-in-hand with labor unions on pieces of legislation. I have supported expanding the right to collective bargain. I have worked on strengthening our prevailing wage and apprenticeship standards.”
Watts still has the backing of several other labor unions, including AFSCME, Clark County Education Association, Nevada State Education Association, and Clark County Firefighters Local 1908.
On his end, Dávila acknowledges the contention between Watts and certain labor groups, but he says his decision to run for office predates those issues.
“There is a history that is definitely fueling some of the support,” he said, “but ultimately this is a campaign about helping working people.”
Dávila downplays the relevance of the thrice failed proposal to massively expand the state’s film tax credit program. He contends the building trade groups did not explicitly ask him about the proposal or how he would have voted on it. (Watts twice voted against the proposed $1.8 billion public subsidy.)
Dávila believes support from those unions stems from being on the same page about reinvestment in the community more broadly.
“We see this as a race much larger than that” single issue, he added.
The candidates
It would be difficult to find a candidate more homegrown than Watts, who was born within the current boundaries of AD15 at Sunrise Hospital to parents who met working at the Desert Inn Casino (where Wynn and Encore resorts are now, also in the district). Watts is a graduate of Las Vegas Academy and University of Nevada, Las Vegas, the latter of which is also located in the district.
Watts’ professional background is in political engagement within the nonprofit sector. He spent several years at the Progressive Leadership Alliance of Nevada until he left to launch his own small business consulting nonprofits.
He ran for AD15 in 2018 and has easily won reelection three times.
Dávila is a Venezuelan immigrant who first moved to Southern Nevada with his family as a teenager. An alumnus of Green Valley High School, UNLV, and the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT), Dávila has worked for the late Sen. Harry Reid as a staff assistant and U.S. Sen. Catherine Cortez Masto as a casework manager.
More recently, he has worked as an urban planner at the Regional Transportation Center of Southern Nevada. It’s a job he says keeps him acutely aware of the intersection of economic development, jobs, transportation, and housing.
Dávila says what drew him to urban planning was “the opportunity to bring public policy and community engagement together to draft very clear and strategic action plans.” But at RTC he has learned that even the best laid plans stay just plans unless they are given the resources to become a reality.
“I want to make sure that we are able to reinvest in our communities, which are often our established neighborhoods, our older neighborhoods, in and around the Las Vegas Strip,” he said.
Watts is known as a champion for environmental protections. Last year, he worked on legislation to allow affordable housing projects to install solar, opening the door for renters to embrace clean energy (and the lower prices that come with it). He has also sponsored bills aimed at keeping NV Energy accountable.
Watts says he has tried to pass bills that are “prioritizing communities and people that often get left behind.”
After constituents relayed their struggles paying Nevada’s high annual vehicle registration fees, Watts successfully led the passage of a bill that will allow people to pay in installments rather than all at once. (The Nevada Department of Motor Vehicles has not yet launched the option.)
Watts also worked on legislation related to craft breweries, an area of interest for the Arts District, which is also located in AD15.
‘Just…the cost of doing business’: Lawmaker blasts scofflaw vibes wafting up from Musk’s tunnels

More recently, as chair of the interim legislative committee on growth and infrastructure, Watts has led the charge on publicly demanding answers about The Boring Company’s Vegas Loop, a series of tunnels underneath the Las Vegas Convention and Visitors Authority and Las Vegas Strip properties. Boring sites have been connected to a high number of alleged occupational and environmental safety violations.
That interim committee highlighted there was a growing backlog of complaints at the OSHA Review Board, and two months later a plan was developed to address the backlog.
Watts is pleased some efforts have been taken, but he says he is still looking ahead to sponsoring policy that ensures the problems don’t reemerge once fewer eyes are watching.
“So it’s not just holding The Boring Company accountable,” he added. It’s “also seeing how we fix these bigger structural problems that can threaten the environment or threaten the health and well being of workers generally.”
When it comes to his legislative agenda, Dávila sees homelessness as “a big priority” and “a failure of urban planning.” He believes the state needs to ramp up housing production and diversify the types of housing available.
“There’s a lot of really innovative and sophisticated urban planning policy that could solve our housing challenges,” he said. “That’s another reason why I’m running. There’s a gap in urban planning policy at the Legislature that really needs to be filled for us to solve some of these very complex problems.”
Dávila said he’s especially interested in land trusts. He’d like to sponsor legislation to enable local and state governments, or a government-sponsored developer, to bid on affordable housing units and create land trusts that protect those units from speculation.
Dávila says he is taking an “urban planning approach” by talking to neighbors about the problems they see and then bringing people together to find solutions to those problems. He says most people he’s met knocking on doors say they are most concerned about standing up to President Donald Trump and ICE, affordability, and transportation.
Both AD15 candidates said they are committed to protecting the state from meddling by the president.
“We’ve got Trump attacking our elections, trying to steal our data, and working to have ICE terrorize our communities,” said Watts.
Watts said the Legislature next year will likely be dealing with the massive cuts spearheaded by the Trump administration.
“We’re going to have to figure out how to deal with that,” he said. “I’ve got experience working through and navigating these challenges. We often talk about policy, but the budget is super important.”
Watts for the last three legislative sessions served on the Assembly Ways & Means Committee — the chamber’s powerful money committee. Assuming he is reappointed to the committee for a fourth time, he would be the most senior member on the committee.
On his end, Dávila says he is ready to take on Trump and Trump’s impact. Dávila, an immigrant, draws a parallel from the Venezuela he and his family left behind in 2006 and what is happening to the United States now.
“There was a threat of authoritarianism. We still had elections, we still had freedom of the press, and universities were independent. But there were very clear threats to all of those institutions.”
Fundraising
Watts has raised significantly more money than Dávila during the first quarter of this year, campaign contribution and expense reports filed with the state show. Watts reported raising $56,000 in the first quarter of the year, compared to $15,000 raised by Dávila.
When combined with their 2025 fundraising, and after expenses, Watts had $332,000 as of April 1. Dávila had $27,000.
Watt’s top donors from this year include Boyd Gaming, Solar Energy Industries Association, and Community Choice Financial, the parent company of TitleMax. Dávila’s top donors were SEIU, LiUNA, and the Operative Plasterers’ & Cement Masons’ International Association (OPCMIA).

name: Delaware
title: Aternium taps Siemens Energy for hydrogen facility design, advancing $1B Mid-Atlantic initiative
description: Siemens Energy will provide advanced hydrogen production technology to improve efficiency, scalability, and environmental performance. WILMINGTON, Del. — Aternium Inc. has selected Siemens Energy as a key partner for the front-end engineering design phase of its planned clean hydrogen production facility, marking a major step forward in the company’s push to[...]
text:
Siemens Energy will provide advanced hydrogen production technology to improve efficiency, scalability, and environmental performance.
WILMINGTON, Del. — Aternium Inc. has selected Siemens Energy as a key partner for the front-end engineering design phase of its planned clean hydrogen production facility, marking a major step forward in the company’s push to build large-scale energy infrastructure in the Mid-Atlantic.
The partnership centers on a Front-End Engineering Design (FEED) study — a critical early planning phase for major industrial projects. During this stage, engineers develop detailed technical designs, refine cost estimates, evaluate safety and environmental requirements, and determine how a facility will be built and operated. The process helps companies reduce risk and make final investment decisions before construction begins.
Aternium said Siemens Energy will provide advanced hydrogen production technology aimed at improving efficiency, scalability, and environmental performance. The companies will work alongside Kiewit Engineering Group, which is currently leading pre-FEED work on the project.
“This phase allows us to optimize and finalize a bespoke design for Aternium to prepare this project for execution,” said Dan Restrepo, head of sales for sustainable energy systems in the Americas at Siemens Energy.
Photo: Andrew Cottone, PhD, Founder and CEO of Aternium
Focus on clean hydrogen and industrial demand
The proposed facility is designed to produce clean hydrogen, a fuel increasingly viewed as essential for reducing emissions in industries that are difficult to electrify, such as heavy manufacturing and transportation.
The FEED study will evaluate engineering standards, safety protocols, and environmental impacts, helping ensure the facility meets regulatory and operational benchmarks.
Aternium’s broader model goes beyond hydrogen production. The company also plans to extract deuterium — also known as heavy water — a specialized material used in nuclear fusion research and critical manufacturing processes, including semiconductors, fiber optics, and pharmaceuticals.
Part of a broader $1 billion regional strategy
The project is part of Aternium’s larger vision to develop a network of hydrogen and heavy water facilities across the Mid-Atlantic, representing an estimated $1 billion investment.
“We are thrilled to embark on this FEED study as it represents a cornerstone of our strategic plan to lead the hydrogen economy,” said Andrew Cottone. “Partnering with Siemens Energy positions us to develop a hydrogen production facility that will reduce emissions in hard-to-decarbonize industries and contribute significantly to the global energy transition.”
Why it matters
Hydrogen has emerged as a key piece of the evolving energy landscape, particularly as states and industries look to balance economic growth with emissions reductions.
Projects like Aternium’s signal growing interest in positioning the Mid-Atlantic — including Delaware — as a hub for next-generation energy production, advanced manufacturing, and supply chain innovation.
Aternium, a U.S.-based company focused on clean hydrogen and heavy water production, was named one of the top 10 startups to watch in 2026 by the Philadelphia Business Journal.

name: Michigan Advance
title: Debbie Stabenow endorses Haley Stevens in U.S. Senate bid
description: A recently retired U.S. senator from Michigan is backing U.S. Rep. Haley Stevens, a big pickup for the congresswoman from Birmingham as she seeks the Democratic nomination for U.S. Senate. Former U.S. Sen. Debbie Stabenow announced Wednesday morning that she was endorsing Stevens. Stabenow served as Michigan’s senator for nearly 25 years. “It was the […]
text:
U.S. Sen. Debbie Stabenow, D-Mich., speaks at an event kicking off the Harris-Walz Reproductive Freedom Bus Tour with the cast of "Scandal" in Madison Heights, Mich., on Sept. 22, 2024. Also on stage is U.S. Rep. Haley Stevens (D-Birmingham). (Photo by Andrew Roth/Michigan Advance)A recently retired U.S. senator from Michigan is backing U.S. Rep. Haley Stevens, a big pickup for the congresswoman from Birmingham as she seeks the Democratic nomination for U.S. Senate.
Former U.S. Sen. Debbie Stabenow announced Wednesday morning that she was endorsing Stevens. Stabenow served as Michigan’s senator for nearly 25 years.
“It was the honor of my lifetime to suit up every day and fight for Michigan as your US senator,” Stabenow said in a statement circulated by Stevens’ campaign. “Today, I’m endorsing Congresswoman Haley Stevens to be our next senator, because I know she’ll do the same thing. Haley was born and raised in Michigan.”
Stabenow said Stevens was “Michigan through and through,” and said Stevens has been a key partner of hers since before Stevens served in Congress and was President Barack Obama’s chief of staff for the auto rescue plan during his first term. 


“Haley has the track record and the Michigan grit to lower costs and get things done for Michigan families,” Stabenow said. “Equally important, at this very critical time, I know she can beat Mike Rogers in the general election. The stakes have never been higher, and Haley Stevens is the right person at the right time for Michigan.”
Stevens thanked Stabenow, noting that “throughout our state’s history, there have been few greater champions for Michigan than my friend Debbie Stabenow.”
“She fought for Michigan manufacturing, protected our Great Lakes and clean water, stood up for our farmers, and took on tough fights–and won for Michigan,” Stevens said in a statement. “Senator Stabenow knows what it takes to win in Michigan and deliver for Michigan, and I’ll continue the incredible work she did for our state in the Senate. I’m honored and humbled to have her on my side in this campaign.”
Stevens is facing a tough primary fight against state Sen. Mallory McMorrow of Royal Oak and former Wayne County health official Abdul El-Sayed.
Stabenow’s backing certainly helps Stevens make her case for the role, as the former senator can now count herself as one of Stevens’ most prominent Michigan-based campaign surrogates.
The winner of the August primary will likely go on to face the presumptive Republican nominee, former U.S. Rep. Mike Rogers of White Lake. Rogers, who is endorsed by President Donald Trump and is the clear frontrunner, still faces a primary challenge from former Michigan Republican Party co-chair Bernadette Smith.

name: Utah News Dispatch
title: Utah’s kratom ban takes effect: Adulterated products should be off shelves starting today
description: Most kratom products won’t be on Utah shelves starting today as new legislation goes into effect allowing only pure leaf powders and capsules to be sold in specialty stores.  A lawsuit from Botanic Tonics, the manufacturer of “feel free” tonics, won’t delay the law. A federal judge denied the company’s request for an injunction on […]
text:
A shop in Salt Lake City advertises kratom for sale on Thursday, Feb. 5, 2026. (Photo by Spenser Heaps for Utah News Dispatch)Most kratom products won’t be on Utah shelves starting today as new legislation goes into effect allowing only pure leaf powders and capsules to be sold in specialty stores. 
A lawsuit from Botanic Tonics, the manufacturer of “feel free” tonics, won’t delay the law. A federal judge denied the company’s request for an injunction on Monday.
Quickly after the Utah Legislature approved a partial kratom ban this year prohibiting adulterated kratom from being sold in the state, the company sued state officials in federal court, asking for a judge to declare the new regulations unconstitutional while arguing it contradicts federal law. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX
Botanic Tonic’s “feel free” tonic mixes kratom and kava root, which according to the new law, will be illegal to sell in Utah as it combines kratom with a “nonkratom” substance. Utah’s law, the company said, would cause them to remove their products from Utah stores and immediately lose over $10.7 million.
However, according to court documents, a judge found the company “failed to show a likelihood of success on their legal arguments that federal law preempts any relevant part of the Kratom Regulation Act.” 
Makers of ‘feel free’ tonics sue Utah officials over new kratom regulations

“Even if feel free falls within the federal definition of a dietary supplement and does not meet statutory criteria for being deemed to be adulterated, these federal statutes do not require that feel free be sold,” the court wrote in its decision. 
That means that even if federal law allows kratom supplements like “feel free,” the company is able to comply with Utah regulations “by simply declining to sell feel free in Utah.” 
Botanic Tonics filed an appeal to the decision on Tuesday. It did not reply to a request for comment.
The kratom leaf, native to Southeast Asia, has been the center of controversy nationally. While many say it’s highly effective in treating conditions like chronic pain, anxiety and opioid use disorders, kratom products can also have opioid-like characteristics and have been responsible for addiction and even death among Utahns.
Lawmakers have discussed at length kratom products’ presence in gas stations and convenience stores, especially studying the impacts of items that increase the herb’s potency by artificially enhancing 7-hydroxymitragynine, or 7-OH, a naturally occurring alkaloid that’s only a minor constituent of the plant.
Senate Minority Assistant Whip Mike McKell, R-Spanish Fork, who sponsored the law and has heavily advocated for a full kratom ban in the state, told Utah News Dispatch he believes the court reached the right conclusion.



Let us know what you think...


 


While the company may have appealed, McKell predicted the company won’t prevail.
“That’s a really bad sign for them, if the court, looking at it at this initial level, doesn’t feel like they have a substantial likelihood of prevailing,” McKell said. “It’s going to be an uphill battle for them, certainly.”
Now that the partial ban is going into effect, McKell said he intends to keep an eye on the issue, hoping for a full ban. But, as of Tuesday afternoon, he said “midnight can’t come soon enough.”
“Bottom line is the product sold by the company Botanic Tonics is really dangerous, and I’m glad that we’re no longer going to be selling the product ‘feel free’ in the state of Utah,” he said. “It is one of the worst, and it didn’t surprise me that they wanted to litigate it, but I’m also glad the court ruled against them.”

title: Drone restrictions bill loaded with dozens of amendments in Missouri House
description: A bill to prohibit low-flying drones over power plants, pipelines and other infrastructure transformed into wide-ranging public safety legislation Tuesday as the Missouri House added 47 amendments over nearly three and half hours. As the debate wore on, the bill became loaded with proposals ranging from a domestic violence registry to expanded DNA testing af[...]
text:
Legislation sponsored by State Sen. Nick Schroer, a Defiance Republican, grew to include amendments ranging from a domestic violence registry to expanded DNA testing after arrests and an expanded pay policy at the state-controlled St. Louis Metropolitan Police Department (Annelise Hanshaw/Missouri Independent).A bill to prohibit low-flying drones over power plants, pipelines and other infrastructure transformed into wide-ranging public safety legislation Tuesday as the Missouri House added 47 amendments over nearly three and half hours.
As the debate wore on, the bill became loaded with proposals ranging from a domestic violence registry to expanded DNA testing after arrests and altering pay policies at the state-controlled St. Louis Metropolitan Police Department.
The underlying bill, sponsored by Republican state Sen. Nick Schroer of Defiance, would expand the law that currently makes it a crime to operate drones over open-air stadiums or concert venues, reducing the minimum size of facilities where restrictions apply from 5,000 to 500 occupants and adding “critical infrastructure.”
The bill started the day at six pages. As House members prepared to vote on the final product, some speculated about its size — and whether the legislation they had rolled into the bill had gotten enough scrutiny.
“If I were a betting man, I would be very curious about the amount of pages that this new bill would be,” said Democratic state Rep. Marty Joe Murray of St. Louis. 
Democratic state Rep. LaKeySha Bosley of St. Louis said some of the bills attached to Schroer’s legislation hadn’t previously been discussed by the House.
“There are a few bills on here that have never been vetted, that didn’t go through the committees, that didn’t have any conversations,” Bosley said. “The first time we had a conversation was on this floor, and only maybe one or two people even dove into the practicality of the bills.”
In the end, the legislation passed the House 83 to 61, with 18 Republicans and 43 Democrats in opposition, receiving just one more “aye” vote than needed to pass. The bill would need Senate approval to go to the governor.
Most of the provisions tacked onto Schroer’s legislation passed with little or no opposition.
One measure would make Missouri the third state, after Texas and Tennessee, to establish a domestic violence offender registry required for people convicted of two or more sexual assaults, felonies or class A misdemeanors against a family or household member.
Rep. Raychel Proudie, a Democrat from Ferguson, speaks on the House floor in Feb. 2025 (Tim Bommel/Missouri House Communications).
Democratic state Rep. Raychel Proudie of Ferguson, one of the sponsors of the bill, said it would prevent repeat offenders from continuing a pattern of abuse.
“This session, we have done a tremendous amount of work for individuals who are survivors or who have succumbed to domestic violence,” Proudie said. “This continues that trend, making sure we are offering public safety options to all victims.”
Legislation sponsored by Republican state Rep. Philip Oehlerking of Ballwin would require the Missouri Department of Corrections to help inmates obtain driver’s licenses or state ID cards and records of their vocational training by the time of their release. 
Oehlerking said the measure would help people find employment and reduce recidivism.
Democratic state Rep. Kimberly-Ann Collins of St. Louis added an amendment, based on legislation she sponsored with Republican state Rep. Jamie Gragg of Ozark, specifying that nonviolent offenders can earn “good time credit” toward their sentences for undergoing drug or alcohol use treatment, earning a high school or college diploma or vocational training certificate, or completing restorative justice.
“They will come out into society to reintegrate and hopefully become good tax-paying, law-abiding citizens,” Collins said.
Another amendment with little opposition would require drunk drivers who are convicted of killing a parent to pay child support for surviving children under 18.
But some of the amendments drew criticism.
A measure sponsored by Republican state Rep. Lane Roberts of Joplin would create the offense of “impeding, threatening or harassing a first responder” if someone goes within 25 feet of an officer or emergency medical provider after being warned not to approach.
While Roberts said the measure would protect first responders and bystanders, some lawmakers argued it would damage law enforcement transparency.
Democratic state Rep. Marlon Anderson of St. Louis said the discussion reminded him of the role of audio and video footage in the conviction of the Minneapolis police officer who killed George Floyd in 2020.
The final words spoken by Floyd in a video taken by a bystander were, “I can’t breathe.”
“But for that audio, that bad actor may have been [ruled] not guilty,” Anderson said.
Another measure, based on a bill filed by Republican state Rep. Cameron Parker of Campbell, would add to the list of offenses when law enforcement can collect DNA samples upon arrest. The additional offenses include drug possession and interfering with arrest.
Democratic state Rep. Elizabeth Fuchs of St. Louis said the legislation could “infringe upon the presumption of innocence.”
Anderson said it would disproportionately impact Missourians of color.
“I believe it’s going to start a fishing expedition for people who look like me,” Anderson said.
Several St. Louis Democrats decried an amendment offered by Republican state Rep. Brad Christ of St. Louis County that would alter language in the law that placed the St. Louis Metropolitan Police Department under state control last year. 
Christ said the amendment would give flexibility to pay overtime to lieutenants in the department. It would also absolve the new Board of Police Commissioners from liability for actions by the department before it was created.
Bosley said the amendment was “absolutely asinine” and argued that it would violate the city’s local rights.
“You broke it,” Bosley said. “You fix it. You pay for it.”
